name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_STATEMENT4_Q01 - Oxidation state evaluation and stock notation rules

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding oxidation numbers and Stock notation:

Statement I: In oxygen difluoride (\(\mathrm{OF_2}\)), the oxidation state of oxygen is \(+2\), whereas in dioxygen difluoride (\(\mathrm{O_2F_2}\)), it is \(+1\).

Statement II: According to Stock notation, auric chloride and stannous chloride are designated as \(\mathrm{Au(III)Cl_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Sn(II)Cl_2}\), respectively.

Statement III: The highest permissible oxidation state for representative main-group elements in group 15, 16, and 17 is numerically equal to their group number.

Statement IV: In carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\)), the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of one carbon atom and three oxygen atoms equals \(-2\).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
According to standard oxidation number assignment rules: fluorine is the most electronegative element and invariably assigned an oxidation number of \(-1\) in all its compounds; German chemist Alfred Stock introduced the system of indicating the oxidation state of a metal in Roman numerals within parentheses after the metal symbol; the maximum positive oxidation number of an element in representative p-block groups never exceeds its valence electrons (equal to group number minus 10); and for polyatomic ions, the algebraic sum of all oxidation numbers must equal the net ionic charge.

Step 2: Evaluation of oxygen fluoride oxidation states
In \(\mathrm{OF_2}\), each fluorine atom is in the \(-1\) oxidation state. Setting \(\text{O} + 2(-1) = 0\) yields \(\text{O} = +2\). In \(\mathrm{O_2F_2}\), setting \(2(\text{O}) + 2(-1) = 0\) yields \(2(\text{O}) = +2\), giving \(\text{O} = +1\). Thus, the assignment of \(+2\) for oxygen difluoride and \(+1\) for dioxygen difluoride is scientifically accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of Stock notation representations
In auric chloride (\(\mathrm{AuCl_3}\)), gold is in the \(+3\) oxidation state, which is represented in Stock notation as \(\mathrm{Au(III)Cl_3}\). In stannous chloride (\(\mathrm{SnCl_2}\)), tin is in the \(+2\) oxidation state, designated as \(\mathrm{Sn(II)Cl_2}\). Thus, both representations follow the Stock convention accurately.

Step 4: Evaluation of maximum oxidation states in p-block groups
For modern IUPAC groups 15, 16, and 17, the valence shell electron counts are 5, 6, and 7, respectively. The maximum oxidation number cannot exceed the valence shell electrons, which equals the modern group number minus 10 (namely \(+5\) for group 15, \(+6\) for group 16, and \(+7\) for group 17), not the group number itself. An oxidation number of \(+15\) or \(+17\) is physically impossible. Therefore, the claim that the highest oxidation state equals the group number is incorrect.

Step 5: Evaluation of algebraic sum rule for polyatomic carbonate
In the carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\)), carbon has an oxidation state of \(+4\) and each oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\). The algebraic sum is \((+4) + 3(-2) = 4 - 6 = -2\), exactly matching the net charge of the divalent anion. Hence, the algebraic sum rule holds true.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The valid assertions are those describing the \(+2\) and \(+1\) oxidation states of oxygen in fluorides, the Stock notations \(\mathrm{Au(III)Cl_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Sn(II)Cl_2}\), and the net charge summation of carbonate, while the claim equating maximum oxidation state to group number is invalid. Therefore, Statement I, Statement II and Statement IV only are correct.

answer.text: Statement I, Statement II and Statement IV only
Statement II, Statement III and Statement IV only
Statement I, Statement II, Statement III and Statement IV

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_REDOXREACTIONS_STATEMENT4_Q02 - Disproportionation halogen displacement and redox reactivity

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements concerning redox transformations and competitive electron transfer:

Statement I: During the preparation of household bleaching agents, chlorine gas undergoes disproportionation in alkaline solution to yield chloride and hypochlorite ions.

Statement II: Addition of concentrated sulphuric acid to a solid bromide salt releases reddish-brown bromine vapours because sulphuric acid oxidises bromide ions.

Statement III: Elemental fluorine can be prepared chemically in aqueous solution by bubbling chlorine gas through sodium fluoride solution.

Statement IV: When a metallic zinc rod is immersed in copper sulphate solution, zinc spontaneously reduces copper(II) ions to metallic copper.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
A disproportionation reaction involves a single element in one oxidation state undergoing simultaneous oxidation and reduction. Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a moderately strong oxidising agent capable of oxidising bromide to elemental bromine. Halogen oxidising power decreases down group 17 (\(\mathrm{F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2}\)); hence, a halogen can only displace heavier halide ions from aqueous solution, never lighter ones. In competitive metal displacement, a more electropositive metal with a lower standard reduction potential displaces a less electropositive metal from its salt solution.

Step 2: Evaluation of chlorine in alkaline medium
When chlorine reacts with dilute aqueous alkali at room temperature, the chemical reaction is: \[\mathrm{Cl_2(g) + 2OH^-(aq) \rightarrow Cl^-(aq) + ClO^-(aq) + H_2O(l)}\] Chlorine starts with an oxidation number of \(0\) and is simultaneously reduced to \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) and oxidised to \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{ClO^-}\). This constitutes disproportionation and forms the basis of household bleaching solutions, verifying this chemical behavior.

Step 3: Evaluation of bromide reaction with concentrated sulphuric acid
When concentrated sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)) reacts with bromide salts, hydrogen bromide formed initially is oxidised by hot concentrated sulphuric acid to elemental bromine: \[\mathrm{2NaBr + 3H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2NaHSO_4 + SO_2 + Br_2 + 2H_2O}\] Sulphuric acid is reduced to sulfur dioxide while bromide (\(-1\)) is oxidised to bromine (\(0\)), releasing reddish-brown vapours. Hence, this oxidation reaction is chemically verified.

Step 4: Evaluation of chemical displacement to generate fluorine
Fluorine is the strongest oxidising halogen due to its high hydration enthalpy, low bond dissociation energy, and high electron gain enthalpy. Its standard reduction potential (\(+2.87\text{ V}\)) is substantially higher than that of chlorine (\(+1.36\text{ V}\)). Therefore, chlorine gas cannot oxidise fluoride ions to elemental fluorine; rather, fluorine spontaneously oxidises water and other halides. Elemental fluorine cannot be prepared by chemical displacement in aqueous solutions and must be produced electrolytically. Thus, the claim describing the chemical oxidation of fluoride by chlorine is incorrect.

Step 5: Evaluation of zinc-copper displacement
The standard reduction potential of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}\) is \(-0.76\text{ V}\), whereas that of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}\) is \(+0.34\text{ V}\). Zinc has a greater tendency to release electrons and is a stronger reducing agent than copper. Consequently, zinc spontaneously displaces copper from \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution (\(\mathrm{Zn(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow Zn^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)}\)). The reverse reaction does not proceed spontaneously. Hence, the displacement behavior is fully justified.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The valid assertions are the disproportionation of chlorine in alkali, the oxidation of bromide by sulphuric acid, and the displacement of copper by zinc, whereas the chemical displacement of fluoride by chlorine is invalid. Therefore, Statement I, Statement II and Statement IV only are correct.

answer.text: Statement I, Statement II and Statement IV only
Statement I, Statement II, Statement III and Statement IV
